existing_record.name: Musique traditionnelle québécoise
existing_record.lineage: Québec's French-Canadian dance and song tradition of the Saint Lawrence valley, documented from the nineteenth century, professionalized by La Bolduc and fiddler Jean Carignan and revived from the 1970s by La Bottine Souriante and Le Vent du Nord — crooked reels and gigues at 110-130 BPM driven by seated podorythmie foot percussion, diatonic accordion and fiddle in unison, ragtime-inflected piano backing, and chansons à répondre with turlutte mouth-music refrains.

existing_extras.description: Traditional Québécois music is the kitchen-party and veillée repertoire of French Canada, built on fiddle-and-accordion dance tunes and responsorial song, and continuously performed rather than reconstructed. Its unmistakable features are podorythmie — the fiddler's own seated foot-tapping as the rhythm section — irregular 'crooked' tune structures with added or dropped beats, a piano accompaniment style borrowed from ragtime and vaudeville, and turlutte vocal mouth-music standing in for instruments. It shares Celtic modal tune shapes with Irish and Cape Breton traditions but is distinguished by the foot-percussion drive, the French song layer, and the tolerance for asymmetrical bar counts that Scottish and Irish repertoires largely regularized away.
